common_themes.summary: Adoption of robotic surgery is growing across all three markets, but access remains uneven and concentrated in larger institutions (larger academic hospitals, private centres, university hospitals, and larger NHS trusts) while smaller regional hospitals or facilities lag behind.

evidence.quote: Adoption is growing, but it is still concentrated in larger academic hospitals and private centres with stronger capital budgets. Smaller regional hospitals are much slower.
It is growing, but adoption is quite uneven. Large university hospitals are much more advanced, while many smaller hospitals are still waiting.
Adoption is increasing, and in some larger NHS trusts robotic surgery is becoming standard for selected procedures. But access still varies significantly by hospital.

common_themes.summary: Hospitals in multiple markets emphasize that training multiple surgeons and theatre staff is critical to maintaining high system utilization and supporting a viable economic business case.

evidence.quote: Training matters, especially in the first year. If only one surgeon can use the system, the economics become difficult. Hospitals want several surgeons trained so utilisation is high enough.
Very important operationally. If the hospital buys a system but only one surgeon is comfortable using it, utilisation will be poor. That weakens the business case.
Funding is important, but I would say training capacity is just as important. You can buy a system, but if you cannot train enough surgeons and theatre staff, adoption stalls.

common_themes.theme: Capital Cycle Dependencies on Purchasing Timelines
common_themes.summary: Purchasing timelines in multiple markets are significantly influenced by capital budget approvals and the timing of capital cycles, which can delay procurement processes.

evidence.quote: Six to twelve months is realistic once the hospital becomes serious. It can be longer if the capital committee pushes the purchase into the next budget cycle.
Around six to nine months can happen if funding is already available. If the trust has to wait for a new capital cycle, it can take much longer.

market_differences.theme: Role of Economics versus Clinical Strategy in Purchasing Decisions
market_differences.summary: The relative weight placed on pure finance and economics versus clinical outcomes and strategy varies across markets during purchasing decisions.

markets.position: Finance teams and purchasing committees require a strong economic case covering utilisation, procedure volume, and maintenance costs, where clinical outcomes alone are not enough if systems offer similar clinical results.
Cost is the primary barrier due to hospital financial pressures, and the economic case, total cost of ownership, service contracts, and expected procedure volume ultimately decide approval.
Economics and clinical strategy are balanced, and purchasing discussions are not purely financial, incorporating patient outcomes, length of stay, and surgeon recruitment.

evidence.quote: Very important. The clinical argument may get surgeons interested, but the finance team wants to understand utilisation, procedure volume, maintenance cost and whether the system will actually pay for itself.

We look at total cost of ownership, expected procedure volume, maintenance, service contracts and training requirements. A strong clinical case helps, but the economic case decides whether it gets approved.
I would say economics and clinical strategy are balanced. I would not say finance alone decides the purchase.

market_differences.summary: Experts across the markets project different trajectories for procedure volume and adoption growth over the medium term.

markets.position: Steady rather than explosive growth, anticipating 15 to 20 percent more procedures annually in stronger centres with slower progress in smaller hospitals.
Gradual growth constrained by competing capital priorities, with procedure volume growth expected closer to high single digits or low double digits.
Positive outlook with potential for acceleration if training expands and systems become more cost competitive, with procedure growth above 15 percent annually in certain areas.

evidence.quote: I expect adoption to continue increasing, probably steadily rather than explosively. I would expect maybe 15 to 20 percent more procedures annually in some of the stronger centres, but smaller hospitals will remain slower.
I would expect continued growth, but probably closer to high single digits or low double digits in procedure volumes rather than something like 20 percent across the whole market.
I am quite positive. I think adoption could accelerate if training expands and systems become more cost competitive. I could see procedure growth above 15 percent annually in some areas.

market_differences.summary: The standard duration for a hospital to purchase a new robotic system differs across the three countries based on alignment and procurement processes.

markets.position: Takes six to twelve months once serious, subject to potential delays from capital committees.
Takes nine to eighteen months as procurement, clinical leadership, finance, and management align.
Takes around six to nine months if funding is already available, though capital cycle waits can extend it.

evidence.quote: Six to twelve months is realistic once the hospital becomes serious. It can be longer if the capital committee pushes the purchase into the next budget cycle.
Nine to eighteen months is common. Procurement, clinical leadership, finance and management all need to align, so it can move slowly.
Around six to nine months can happen if funding is already available. If the trust has to wait for a new capital cycle, it can take much longer.
